en: *Triratnasaundaryagāthā*. Homage to the illustrious Guru Gaṇeśa!

Homage to that Sun-like Guru, by the rays of whose grace the darkness is dispelled by the surrounding radiance of the jewel of the true nature of the self; and thus, with unclouded vision, people behold it clearly and with great expansion. 1.

May that which is known as the glorious Triple Gem—bestower of great bliss, the refuge of all beings, the dispeller of the darkness of poverty for the wise, and the embodiment of beautiful joy—endure for a hundred autumns upon the surface of this earth; may it be a light spreading in all directions, born from the ocean-like lineage of Śrī Pṛthvinārāyaṇa, and possessing an unbroken course.
(1) Taking sovereignty from Indra, majesty from Agni, wrath from Yama, and wealth from Vaiśravaṇa,
as well as the power of creation and maintenance from Rāma and Janārdana, [the Creator] fashions the body of kings.
May the Nepalese Padmapāṇi, Śākyasiṃha, and Svayambhū protect the lineage of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gorakṣācala. 4.
There was a king named Sāhadeva Narabhūpāla, who attained the dawning of grace through the favor of Nepāleśvara and Gorakṣeśvara.
One of that king’s queens slept comfortably upon his bed and, in a dream, told her husband, "I have swallowed the orb of the sun. (5)
(2) Under the pretext of being enraged by faults awakened from sleep, she passed the night crying out as if unable to endure her co-wife;
having cast off the elder child in the womb, she quickly gave birth after seven months to Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, who was equal in qualities to him and was Nārāyaṇa himself in visible form.

(3) Desiring to conquer Nepal, he made it his sole force, filled with secret stratagems as if with arrows, and set forth joyfully and fearlessly like a hunter after a deer. Thus have I heard from another source; that has been described here by me in brief. Does one who establishes the true nature [of things] feel shame in describing Nārāyaṇa? || 7 ||
(4) Having taken refuge in the glorious Mahāmaṇḍapa at Bhairavī on the Traiśūla-Gaṅgā, the illustrious Vāsudeva Pṛthvinārāyaṇa shone forth while residing in Nuwākōṭ. 8.
(5) As soon as he was born, the lion cub did not take the breast;
instead, he cast his gaze toward the grove abounding in elephants.
Having conquered the frontier villages and towns and having made their inhabitants followers of the straight path,
he established military encampments on the banks of Viṣṇumatī, the most excellent of rivers.
(6) He besieged Kīrtipur with arrows having downward-pointing and upward-pointing tips in battle;
it was filled with stone-coffers being carried atop its exceedingly high ramparts.
Then a tumultuous battle took place between those various [demons] with faces turned downward and faces turned upward,
and those standing above with their trees and rocks, against the children, women, and elders who were at the front.

The rain of iron arrows, slings, and stones was so abrasive that it acted like a fire from a cleft; even hundreds of trees, scorched by that fire, stood reduced to mere charred posts, still inspiring terror.
Even now at night, those heroes who bore armor crushed by stones stand as headless trunks with bodies smeared in blood; they weep piteously, mourning for their kinsmen. (14)
Hawks, owls, crows, vultures, ravens, jackals, and even hyenas immediately become joyful and satisfied by means of warm flesh mixed with blood and fat. (15)
(7) Those heroes who were at the forefront of the battle approached the vicinity of the gate; yet, crushed by the impact of showers of stones, they quickly released their lives.
Daily oppressed by the stones, they become like a bed of grass, just as the army of Yudhiṣṭhira was when its body was tormented by the arrows of Bhīṣma.

Having thus seen his own army standing lowly as its rival in battle, Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, as if despondent at the prospect of breaking through the enemy's ramparts, desired to produce many kinds of wealth— namely weapons and missiles— to ensure the success of that war, out of eagerness for those wealthy men who could provide them.

(8) Accompanied by his assembled hosts of ministers, along with the joy of his fame won by his younger brothers—the heroes known as the Pārthas and others—and further joined by the celestial majesty of Kīrtipura, he flooded the Śrīdevīghāṭa and immediately entered the great pavilion; yet, having been humiliated in battle for five or six years due to the defeat of his powerful warriors, he remained deeply dejected.
(9) Weapons and missiles, armor suitable for heroes, and battle-axes; sharp daggers, scissors, as well as wooden planks, tridents, spears, and bhalla-arrows.
There he saw a worm, the size of a thumb, born from a heap of impurities, being forcibly dragged away by hundreds of swarms of ants;
bitten repeatedly by ants, tooth against tooth, the leader was being carried off by the ants to their own hole where they dwell, having fallen from his sixth [birth].

(10) Having reflected upon the relative strength and weakness of his own forces compared to those of the enemy for the sake of destroying the foe, the illustrious Pṛthvinārāyaṇa addressed his own army:
"O soldiers, take only the good qualities [of the enemy]; do not look at the worm. Go once again to Kīrtipurikā for the protection of my fame."
(11) The three worlds—enemies, friends, and neutrals—became like a timid woman upon seeing the forest of the city of his fame reduced to nothing but its pillars. 22.
The Sun-like Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, having first invaded the land of Nepal, entered into fame by piercing the horns of the gods with his sword for seven years;

then, aiming at the illustrious Vyāghra, that conqueror of the ancients—born of a king among men—triumphed by offering a sacrifice to him with the warm flesh from the severed noses of the citizens dwelling in that city. (23)

(12) As the lord of the herd stood firm, having fought for seven years, they all— perceiving him through the influence of their mental impressions to be Śrī Vyāghrabhairava, as clear as crystal— led him to the city with great festivities preceded by prostrations.
And it has been said: "Exertion, daring, fortitude, strength, intelligence, and valor—if these six abide in one, even a god fears him. (25)
(13) And he suddenly afflicted the one-eyed [Rudra], who possesses the majesty and audacity of a hero leading the vanguard in battle,
just as some base man might afflict the breast of a noble woman who, though once married to a king, has ceased to cause him pain.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa... was struck down by Kālopāṇḍi, the commander-in-chief born in the city of Kīrtipura. || 27 ||

Out of that audacity, this Narayana of the king’s earth suddenly attacked a man who had not yet reached his fifth year, along with plundered wealth, as if he were a betrayer of trust, while his nose was severed. (28)
(14) Together with his allies, Saṃserraṇa, Kālūrāṇa, Dalamarda, Sahāyaka, Dalajit, Sāhatula, Rāma, and Bhaṇḍārin, he then set out for the sake of the sinless one. 29.
Śrī Viśvanātha Miśreśa performed a sacrifice of battle,
giving away all his possessions as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), just like the Saptāha Bhāgavata.

(15) He commenced the Viśvajit sacrifice, in which his entire possession was given as the sacrificial fee; for the acquisition of the virtuous is indeed for the sake of renunciation, just like the gathering of water by the clouds.
Satisfied by that sacrifice in which his entire possession was given as the excellent sacrificial fee, Vyāghreśvara bestowed upon King Pṛthvīnarāyaṇa—
the Narāyaṇa among men— the accomplishment of imperial sovereignty, consecrated by the sweat-water trickling from his limbs, which releases one from the bonds of the individual soul.
By Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, who received grace through a dream,
the forests are illuminated just as they were by Raghu.
Just as a deer with a wounded leg is suddenly cornered by a greedy hunter lying in wait, so too was the threefold realm of Nepal suddenly besieged. 34.

(16) Kabandha has long been wakeful; even now he pursues Gaṇeśa from Kīrtipura, as if roaring at his rivals. Grasping his sword at night, he seems to abandon the mutual clash [of blades] through the sounds of his whetted gasps, which act as echoes.
Lokeśvara, Hayagrīva, Bhairava, the Yoginīs of the sacred seats (pīṭha), Ānandādi Lokanātha, and Karkoṭa, the lord of serpents. || 36 ||
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa according to the prescribed rites,
King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa bathed in the waters of the Prabhāvatī.
(17) King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, whose valor illuminated the three worlds, shone resplendent like Vāmana. 38.
The protector of the earth, Bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ, became like the demon Bali before Malla; his head was bowed by the pressure of [Malla’s] feet, and he was overcome by the six principal [qualities]. (39)
And it is said: Rāma drank the Soma at the sacrifice, gave away cows, and performed a wonder;
he honored the priests and brought great Brahmins to Puṇḍarīka with royal humility.
Then there was one whose chief concern was Kālidāsa, who, like Śukrācārya, was distracted from his mind;
he was a whisperer, a slanderer, and a wicked person. (41)
(18) Having made the three kings— those consisting primarily of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— of the nature of *sattva*,
and having made the wrestlers of the nature of *tamas*, he delighted the subjects with *rajas*.
Desiring to adorn his head, he seized the various golden crest-jewels situated upon the pinnacles of the palaces with the intent to wear them as ornaments.
Ṭaudhīdhana and others incited the Tibetan thieves; for, with the consent of the six chief ministers, they instigated those who caused affliction to the country. (44)
And it has been said: "Where the king himself is a thief, accompanied by his army and retinue, what can I do there? For where there is protection, there is fear. (45)
Even though you are a mere subject of the king, you oppress us in vain;
like a swarm of ants, you shall reap the fruit of this meanness. || 46 ||
(19) "He who, having overstepped the path of his own country, should venture into another land— he alone shall be punished," thus he caused a proclamation to be made.
Then, due to mutual conflict, there arose wrestlers,
arsonists, poisoners, those with weapons in hand, and plunderers of wealth.
He himself became a robber of fields and wives, as well as an assailant.
(20) A bad wife destroys the household; a family is destroyed by a bad son;
a bad minister destroys the king; and a kingdom is destroyed by a thief. 49.
(21) Having silently subdued the wrestler Viśvajit with the approval of the Six, he brought his wife alone to his own palace without causing her any injury to the nose.

Thus, they understood that the surface of the earth was subject to the Six through their creation, destruction, and maintenance, for the sake of quelling the suspicion regarding his dual nature. || 50 ||
(22) By means of a deceptive grant of the kingdom, they established Lalitādhipati as the son of the human king named Dalamardana.
For that king restrained each of his sons individually for the sake of his vow,
lest there arise the transgression of the sovereign lord of the gods.
With the consent that the earth would come under the subduing of his enemies, King Jayaprakāśa exiled his own servant from his kingdom; seeking refuge, that man approached Kālidāsa. (53)
Standing at the window of his quadrangular palace, King Dalamaīrdana, visible to the world, beheld Kālidāsa on the royal roads surrounded by his attendants;

he saw him holding a battle-axe in his right hand, a sweetmeat (*modaka*) in the other, and his own trunk—after observing him for the duration of a single blink of an eye, he realized that it was indeed he within the palace.

(23) After serving for some days, that evil-minded personal servant and foot-massager, perceiving that Kālidāsa was sleeping soundly and unsuspectingly, suddenly struck off his head with a sharp axe, saying, "By the king's command! He then departed quickly for the city of Kāntipura; and the king, being pleased, granted him his heart’s desire.

(24) Those six chief ministers assembled together and rushed toward the illustrious king, crying out in haste: "Why do you rage? You are a source of transgression and a creator of famine through cotton!
If it is so, we shall dethrone this devoted one; forgive this sovereignty! Thus they loudly consecrated the lord of men named Śrī Tejaḥmalla.
(25) Dalamardana, perceiving that the governance of the kingdom would be easy for the Pṛthvīnarāyaṇas, wrote that audacious plan;
then, having quickly resolved upon it in his mind, the king set out from his own territory toward the hosts of Nepalese.

(26) There was a king named Jayāditya, who was like a wrestler against the deceptive Hālāhala poison; having spread throughout the entire surface of his palaces and the quarters of the earth medicinal herbs for burning away his enemies, he became terrified at the mere mention of the number of the hosts of Gūrjara kings’ armies.
Fleeing in all directions, he quickly vanished along with his assembly of ministers into the city of Bhaktapura during the night.

(27) While the joyful Pāṇḍutulārāmakas were ascending the palace with its latticed turrets to behold the Queen of the Sovereign of Kings upon the upper floor, their bodies were suddenly consumed by the flames of fire through the power of that medicinal herb; yet those heroes went to the imperishable state. Alas, my friend, the course of destiny is indeed wondrous!

The ritual for the worship of the maiden (*kumārīpūjā*) is described in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā*: "Ornaments, fine silken garments, vermilion, red lac, betel nuts, mirrors, well-known fans made of palm leaves, and small bags."
A small mat, a support for ritual implements,
a cloth garment, a bench, a swing, a doll, along with a conch shell, sandals, and two family lineage-banners.
A caṇḍātaka garment for wrapping, as well as a vessel for ointments, a bed, a pillow, a couch, caskets, and a dressing box.
The time for receiving gifts, the period of the *sīmanta* rite, and likewise the month of *cārtika*;
as well as yellow orpiment, musk, camphor, and saffron.
O beautiful one, other such items as these, as many as one is able,
should be given so that the maiden may be satisfied.
Also in the *Yāmala*: "The mantra-practitioner who always worships a maiden on all festival days—by him the Great Goddess is truly worshipped; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."

(28) On the day of the pilgrimage to Śrīkaumārī, with great festive zeal, incense, and fasting—may there be well-being! May the glory of the illustrious Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa rise through the merit of his incomparable and radiant fame! 60.

Surrounded by six types of attendants— noble men, the wise, the wealthy, the powerful, those conversant with great machines, mantras, and medicinal herbs, and those foremost among whom was Kālidāsa— he,
having crushed Tejomalla in an instant like the demon Cāṇūra, entered Maṇipura like the glorious Nārāyaṇa entering the Madhu forest.

(29) Desiring to seize the realm of Bhakta, the King first made the three lords of the three worlds subjects of the belly of Kālī; thereafter, having caused the King of Kāśī to be defeated in battle, and then having cast aside another king, Āryātīrtha, who had lost his life, as well as Tejamalla, who was perished and seized by poison—the King named Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa is victorious.

(30) When eighty-eight years have passed and the sun of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa has forcibly set behind the lordly mountain of the western quarter, the glimmers of the fireflies that were the kings of the Malla lands shall vanish from the eastern mountain range. That land known as Nepal shall remain stable, and in the hearts of the people there shall abide a sense of wonder and delight born from the fall of the Mallas.

(31) When Goraṣeśa was the lord of the Nepalese land, there was food in abundance even where no grain-measure existed, milk flowed from a vessel that required no milking, and fine garments appeared even where there were no looms. 64.

The king joyfully worshipped, in due order, the illustrious Śākyamuni, the Conqueror of the Three Worlds, and Maitreyanātha; then the Caityas and various distinguished Stūpas, as well as the monasteries beginning with Hanumān; then Hārītī, Śītalā, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and finally Śrī Kṛṣṇa, along with Hara, Bhīmasena, and others.

Thus, having brought the surface of the earth under his own sway, the illustrious Pṛthvinārāyaṇa, by good fortune, imitated the amputation of the hands of the city of Copur as a punishment commensurate with its offense.

Having conquered this earth without a formal battle, he set out on the expedition to Uvākoṭa, just as Nārāyaṇa, after conquering Kaṃsa and witnessing the conduct of the people of Nepāla, proceeded toward Mathurā.

(32) The king did not speak what was improper, untimely, or unbecoming; for he considered it truly excellent that the people should cease from their worldly activities to serve the shrine situated in the city of Lalita.
The king himself commanded the master architect, who was engaged in various wonderful artistic crafts, to build a residence named Vasantapura.
(33) There was no one else on the face of the earth so skilled in all arts and the like as that brahmin Harivaṃśaka, who was endowed with pure artistic intelligence. (68)

On an auspicious day, having laid out the ground according to the principles of architecture, Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa— delighted and desiring to please the goddess Śrī Bhairavī— began the construction of Devīghāṭ, employing masters from Nepal who were experts in the arts of working with stone, crystal, bone, ivory, magnetite, clay, and other materials.

(34) In the beautiful land of Nepal, which has surpassed both gods and men, there are five foremost nectars. Like the Vajra[-family] Yoginīs, these intoxicating and unruly women—whose widowhood is unknown due to the power of Śrī Guhyeśvarī—are given the initiation of "falling" (apātitya-dīkṣā) by the former kings of Nepal; possessing superior strength even over men, these women revel in passion.

In the beautiful land of Nepal, seated at the doors of their respective homes, with their hair tied in braids, possessing lovely faces and adorned with sindūra on their foreheads, the young women—garlanded with flowers and with the corners of their eyes slightly curved—speak with joined palms in sweet, charming words: "Be gracious, O Mother! 71.

"In that region, the supreme seat of Nepal, where Hara is intent on the dance of Siddhi, which abounds in festivals at the temples of various deities and is surrounded by sacred fords and secondary shrines; where the people are impassioned by the chariot procession of the Lord of Fishes (Matsyendra); this is the blessed Lalitāpurī," thus spoke Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa. (72)
I daily bow to that Lord of the World, whom the Vaiṣṇavas call Viṣṇu, the Śaivas call Śiva, the Śāktas call Śakti,

the worshippers of the Sun call the Maker of Day, the twice-born call the embodiment of Brahman, the sages constantly call Matsyendra, and the enlightened call him the Lord of the World— he who is the very essence of compassion. (73)

(36) That person who drinks the excellent *subīja* [milk] from a *pālāśa* leaf, consecrated with the six syllables and empowered by ten million recitations of the *Dīpinī*, for him the letters *ya-ra-la-ma* become sparse.

Oh, how blessed! On the day of the bird (*śikhin*), the lunar mansion of Yama (*yāmyarkṣa*), and the ninth lunar day (*tithi*)—during the journey and other rites—he becomes the Lord of the World; may that God protect us daily from misfortune. 74.
When the charioteer, skilled in his craft, commanded, "Pull quickly! during his departure, the quarters of the sky were filled with the cries of "Hai! Hai! Hā! Hā! Hāhā! Hāhā!
uttered loudly by those striving to pull the ropes, sounding like the roar of thunderclouds; may that very Lord of the World, the crest-jewel of the gods, grant you auspiciousness.

(37) Even when the yoke is broken, when the wheels of the chariot sink low or the chariot is overturned, or when the excellent man seated in the celestial vehicle has steadied himself with his staff firmly grasped;
then, being heralded by the sounds of great kettledrums and the roar of thundering clouds, may this Matsyendranātha, the crest-jewel of the gods, grant you auspiciousness.
Thus, recollecting that festival of Lalitodbhava which brings such bliss, on the eighth lunar day of the month of Pauṣa, during the transit of the sun into Capricorn, and on a Tuesday,
the excellent king Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa caused the acquisition of the Gaṅgā at the great site of Devīghāṭ, upon the pure ground protected by the illustrious Bhairavī.
(38) Thus, whoever here listens with devotion to this life-story of King Śrī Pṛthvinārāyaṇa, poverty remains far from him, and his ancestral sins are indeed destroyed.

(39) He shall become a supreme friend even to the Three Jewels; freed from minor ailments, long-lived, endowed with fortune, a bestower of happiness upon his own family, and accompanied by all [auspicious] groups. 78.
Thus ends the glorious *Pṛthvīnārāyaṇacaritra*.
Born from him was the illustrious King Siṃhapūrvapratāpa, an ornament among sovereigns, who protected his father’s command and illuminated the entire surface of the earth through statesmanship.

Having established the bounds of propriety, he won over the land with taxes and delighted the citizens through his conduct; accompanied by his loyal minister Keherasiṃha, he shone forth, honoring the elders of the city. (79)
(40) He granted a fourth part of the fields to the subjects in the human settlements; thereafter, he had a copper plate inscribed with four names: *Doṣica* and *Auli*.

Victorious is the illustrious King Siṃhapratāpa, whose fame even today exists in embodied form throughout the three worlds, removing misfortune and never failing to provide his own people with cooked food. 80.

(41) Then King Śrī Siṃhapratāpa—by nature gentle, following the conduct of his preceptors, and blessed with great energy—along with the Kāmbojas and the Somanatis, and accompanied by many silver coins, auspiciously caused the practice of using silver coins to follow the custom of the Malla kings. || 81 ||
Born from that [lineage], like a victorious lord of beasts, King Aṇubahādura Sāha— having bestowed the burden of sovereignty upon his son Gīrvāṇayudhanṛpati for one and a half years,
and having assumed the title of "Svāmī"— was a sovereign such as has never existed before, does not exist now, nor will ever exist again, possessing a form so formidable.

In his childhood, he shone as one who, though free from possessiveness, bore the burden of the earth entrusted to his arms; in his youth, having conquered the world through heroic combat, he shone as a sovereign emperor; in his prime, he delighted while the surface of the earth was offered for battle against the illustrious Gīrvāṇas; and in his old age, with the burden of the earth entrusted to Bhīma, he lived in serene repose. (83)

By the command of the illustrious Siṃhapratāpa Ātmaja Raṇabahādura Sāh, the noble crown prince Bāhādura, son of Śrī Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, a long pedestal was fashioned and installed above the window with variegated bricks and wood from sandalwood trees, bearing an image of Ardhanārīśvara accompanied by the host of planets. (84)

(43) For the pleasure of his beloved Īśvarī, King Raṇabahādura—the son of Śrī Siṃhapratāpa—presented today a bell, white as the waves of the celestial river Gaṅgā, resembling a peak of Mount Kailāśa, whose single divine sound strikes fear into bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and ḍākas; it was fashioned from the eight metals by a master smith. 85.

In order to attain liberation from those who consume marrow, fat, grease, entrails, blood, and vital fluids, the illustrious King Raṇabahādūra Sāha— the son of Siṃhapratāpa and a sovereign ruler— contemplated the great and terrifying Śarabhamukha Mahābhairava, who is mounted upon yoga and is not excessively fierce, so as to satisfy his own desire for sovereignty while being greedy for wine, meat, and the like, even as he offered a weight of gold.

(44) Protecting those known as Mālyavājin, Vṛṣabha, and Parivṛḍha—whom he called by the name Nandin—just as the illustrious Maheśvara protects the lords of the Pramathas, the illustrious Mahīśa shone resplendent.

(45) With his discernment in medical treatment cultivated by physicians named Sāṇḍhya, he [tended] to the cattle with balls of food consisting of camphor, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, agallochum, jaggery, the three pungents, and ghee. 87.

The illustrious King Aṇubahādūra Sāha, acting as a diligent protector, provided food appropriate for each species to tigers, bears, monkeys, elephants, horses, deer, nyankus, gokarṇas, rhinoceroses, sāranga antelopes, cakravākas, cranes, peacocks, lizards, quails, pigeons, wolves, dogs, rabbits, rats, and cats. (88)

(46) From the royal capital of Almōḍhā, extending as far as Bammāsāha of the same lineage, and reaching from Kāntīpura to Anumiti for a distance of eight *krośas*, this illustrious and glorious lord Pratāpāraṇabahaḍūrasāha—possessing auspicious fortune, renowned in all four directions, and like Raghu, a lamp to the lineage of Dilīpa—has erected this pillar of victory. 89.

That king was a hero, a lion among men, possessed of ministers devoted to the welfare of both [sides], wise and steadfast, a high-souled one whose fame pervaded the entire world like that of Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, and whose character was formidable;
like the ocean filled with jewels of aquatic creatures, he was unassailable yet accessible to his servants through his multitude of most fierce and lovely royal virtues. (90)

With his feet split by the hooves of Hari’s herd, his nostrils like those of a monkey, and his face distorted, this physician Saṃdhyavaidya became the lord of the cattle, wandering within the forest of his master’s mind. (47) 91.

(48) The royal preceptor Śrī Raṇabahādura became like Hayagrīva; he was a portion of Nirvāṇa, a boiling oil of poison for the wicked, and for distinguished men, he was one who crushed poverty and sin. From a portion not inferior to that [of Nirvāṇa], the King of the Gods (Indra) was born in this world. 92.

Just as one lamp, following after another lamp fed with ghee and a fine wick, shines forth with equal flame and dispels even the blinding, thick darkness; so too, from the great lamp-like King Raṇabaha, the illustrious King Yuvan, whose noble fame was made radiant by the flames of that great lamp, shone forth from afar.

(49) Out of affection, when his third year had passed, he was consecrated to the imperial sovereignty inherited from his father, Raṇabahādūra. Possessing the state of supreme Śiva-nirvāṇa which is attainable only by the lords of yogins, he bore the name Mahānandasvāmī throughout the circle of the earth. 94.

(50) Having led the king—who was devoted to the sport of hunting—to Anuvākoṭa, the treacherous ministers, alas, placed their lord—the foremost warrior among the gods, an abode of compassion, and one intent on the bliss of liberation—into the eight-petaled lotus [of the cremation ground] in his eightieth year, while he was a resident of Lalitapura. 95.

(51) Whatever has been inscribed by the Creator and the lords of the earth—whether it be false or true—is certain to bear fruit in its own time, whether in a desert or on Mount Meru; this is not at all surprising.
(52) A queen cannot be cured even by world-renowned physicians who are experts in medical science and equal to the sage Caraka or Dhanvantari. 96.
In the destruction of his virtuous, brave subjects, he bestowed upon thousands of cattle-herds, along with land and ritual fees, a share for every year;
he caused elephants to be paraded in their respective colors beneath the shade of parasols at the crossroads with their thrones, and he had the propitiatory rites recited.
(53) In the temple of Śiva, in the house of the dead, on the surface of the earth, on the ground, in rivers, at confluences, and furthermore in water-channels and wells;
in the abodes of Machindranātha, Mīnanātha, and Śākyasiṃha; together with Bhīmasena, joyfully, in Narāyaṇa, and with Kṛṣṇa. 98.
Then, at the Gaṇeśas and Bhairavas, as well as at the city gates, that king of yogis performed, according to his own Vedic branch, the ritual rites along with the Rudrīya hymns for each caste.
Furthermore, every day during the monthly courses of the wives of the kings, he fed the assembly of yogis and yoginīs.
"An unprecedented reward has been proclaimed for those who bring the sky-dwellers from the air, captured with snares and bound by various mechanical devices, so that their death may occur;

or else, he who shall bring them alive—even if it be my own son—to him I shall grant whatever he desires. Thus was the sincere command issued by the lords of the kings regarding the capture of the vultures. (100)
(54) Having cremated the vultures, the high-souled Lord King then became happy. Such a battle of vultures had never before entered the range of hearing, nor had it ever been seen.

Even today, the place where [the vulture] fell remains; thus it has been told by those of advanced wisdom and mature age, who are skilled in acting for the benefit of children, that a voice was established there due to the possession of a spirit. 101.
Then, like Bhairaveśa, Naravāha became possessed of divine vision like the King of the Gods;
thereafter, he joyfully commanded the five classes of weapon-bearers to come into his presence.
(55) Wherever he was carried by human vehicle, there indeed he established a good reputation;
delighted, he presented artificial groves and herds of animals to the Lord. 103.
The lord of Raṇabhūdhara also established grazing grounds for his cattle,
and he bestowed the earth upon Vedic scholars for a distance of one yojana on all sides, in order to remove their ailments.

The lord of Raṇabhāṭapura, his wrath increased by the wounds [he had received], cut down the Karṇavīra trees in the nearby cemetery, commanding: "Let those who have done him harm flee from here! (105)
(56) Desiring to report her husband’s anger, that mistress named Kanakavatī, filled with indignation, departed from the mortal world as if to go into the assembly of the Three-eyed Lord. 106.
Desirous of burning the dwellings of the physicians' bodies like a pitiless forest fire, the king,
his wrath intensified by grief, ordered a violation of the customary rites of hospitality.
Considering him to be Śiva known as Kumbha despite his most terrible form, the king—
his wrath increased by grief— ordered that a multitude of *aśvakarṇa* trees be brought for the purpose of incense.

Neither by the intense breezes from sandalwood and camphor mixed with agallochum, nor by the cool waters and the air raised by fans and chowries, nor by the consoling conversations and kind words of the courtiers, scholars, kinsmen, and subjects, was the heat of King Raṇabahādura dispelled. (109)

(57) Alas, although the heat of Raṇabahādura—fanned by the words concerning the valor of the gods, the speech of the lord of kings, and Uddhava, which served as nectar—was sprinkled with the fuel of separation from his beloved, it did not subside; for he bore, as it were, a dark spot upon the moon, in the form of his dear tunic. 110.
"Why indeed do you not give me blows from the drum? Alas, the drum bursts, becoming heated by the fire of grief!
For what purpose is this mockery of the drum-beating, O Lord of the forest? Oh, my beloved has gone; where is she? Lead me there after her! || 111 ||

(58) Thus lamenting day after day for a long time, the Lord, having developed true discernment, cast off his outer garment with a mind free from possessiveness; like a goat, he remained awake as before until the great light [of dawn] appeared, and then, with a resolute heart awakened, he instantly performed that upward flight toward Indumatī.
"O dear ones, every day Raṇabahādura Sāh rises to Pūlacoka;
and having mounted that very mortal vehicle, what do those skilled in reflection say about it? (113)
Once, on an auspicious day, having risen early in the morning and perceived favorable omens,
he set out toward the southern direction to go to the city of Dhundhirāja.
(59) In this Kali age, people are corrupt and their very natures are adverse; therefore, for the sake of spiritual merit, I shall seek refuge in the illustrious Lord of the Universe.
Formerly, my father’s venerable feet, known as Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, used to bathe in the waters of the Gaṅgā and then duly worshiped the Lord of the Universe.

(60) "That he [my father] swiftly conquered the land of Nepal through his supreme grace, and that this [city] was established by his feet—remembering this again and again, King Raṇabahādura went to Kāśī, which is inaccessible even to kings, following the passing of Queen Kanakavati. 116.
When his master had gone far away, this jewel among ministers, Anuvaramsi Simha, along with his younger brothers and his army led by Bhima and others—
just as Saumitri followed Rama, the son of Dasharatha, when he was filled with anxiety— then became the companion of his lord.
Then many people, who delighted in equal happiness with him, were devoted to his leadership, attached to him, and indifferent toward their own retinues, followed after him.

(61) Furthermore, the treacherous minister, having gathered together and being intensely devoted to his great ambition, immediately brought the king from even ten million leagues away to the city of Kānti. 118.

The illustrious Svāmirāja, a crest-jewel among kings whose battles were with the gods, shone forth even while his father—the preeminent lord of Aṅga—resided in Kāśī; he bore the burden of the kingdom like his father.

Though he was well-acquainted with the feet of his father, he became an emperor through the imperial fortune, protected by queens who were devoted to the true dharma, and possessed the prosperity of the thousand-armed Kārtavīryārjuna. || 119 ||
He is a child yet possesses the prowess of the non-child; like Hari, he is the uplifter of the earth; through justice, he is like Yama to those with malicious minds;

and like the Lord of the Gods, he is the sovereign of battle. He wields power like the son of the six mothers (Skanda); he is the lord of all classes like the son of two mothers (Kārttikeya); and like Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, his range of vision extends over thousands.
Then the maidservants named Ajayrekhā, Mātūbhrama, and Kalikā, as well as those from Turakīmukha— like ḍākinīs, their mouths fragrant with the scent of wine—
took the Great Queen to Kāntipura from the Kaṭahara forest and acted at will as gatekeepers in the king’s palace.
(63) Although he had previously set out with effort from the Kaṭahara forest, the embodied Dhavaladalaśaśin shone brightly while being protected by Queen Rājalakṣmī out of maternal affection;
yet the illustrious Gīrvāṇayuddha, the ornament of kings, whose heart was filled with longing for the arrival of the glorious Lord of the Earth, did not approve of him in his mind.

Hail! Having attained the lotus feet of his venerable father, the illustrious Mahārāja Gīrvāṇeśa bestowed immeasurable lands upon the gods of the earth and the learned; yet he governed the kingdom—which was like a mere servant—under the name Janakaraṇabahādūrasāha.
Constantly reminding [his subjects] of this, and even making them forget it, he bore the burden of kingship along with its army, causing wonder at every turn.

And it is said in the Bhāṣā: "O friend, when the burden was heavy, you carried it; now that the world has become difficult for everyone, you have become full of remorse. Afterward, you spoke only one word: 'The Lord dwells in Kāśī. But what will happen when you meet the Franks? You have built a house upon the burden; what will be your fate in this world? (124)

How many have lost their wealth gambling at night? How many have been defeated in battle? Who speaks words of defiance without hesitation? How many are exceedingly joyful? And who suffers day and night? Whose heart burns with fever? Whose very water has dried up? Who fills a casket? Standing one by one, everyone in this world remains in a state of manifold conditions. || 125 ||
O King Raṇabahādura Śāha, you are like a pillar of support for this world; O Gīrvāṇarāja of Kāśī, you bestow gifts every day—how wise you are!
(65) You honor the Brahmins from distant lands with various kinds of offerings and hospitality; O King, as you bestow great wealth upon them, your fame spreads far and wide. 126.
Having bathed daily in the waters of the Gaṅgā, Raṇabahādūrasāha became like a golden cloud and a wish-fulfilling tree for the day;
considering himself very fortunate before the venerable Viśveśvara, he bowed with unprecedented humility, offering the means for the illustrious royal prosperity.

Then, being praised by the awakened sons of Gaṅgā in his very presence, the illustrious Lord—like another incarnation of Hayagrīva obtained by Śrī Viśveśa, naturally beautiful, and accompanied by Duṇḍirāja and Lolārka—repeatedly chants the name of the refuge, Viśvanātha. 128.
(66) At that time, even the Europeans residing in Kāśī, regarding the Lord King as their own protector, acted like servants and offered consolation from all sides with many titles;
for the sake of astonishing them with the taste of the various nectars of the flavors of Nepal, they performed acts of honoring the Lord that were more beautiful than the splendor of an empire.
Then the heroic Bhīmasena, whose intellect was as sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, perceived through his reasoning that the entire jewel-studded crown was agitated and largely concealed;

having repeatedly sought forgiveness from the illustrious Lord Viśveśvara with great compassion—the grace of whom provides the path for destroying obstacles while standing at the forefront—he brought the King, his master, back to the city in an instant.
O Bhīmasena, that man, surrounded by spies and employing the methods of conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force, discovered the path of yoga leading out from Kāśī.
Having taken the name Sarparājipadavī (the state of being the queen of serpents), having made his body the object of a series of joys,
and having protected every well-adorned path, he thoroughly understood the path of yoga.

(67) Turning the ocean into dry land, making the earth appear as a mere depression, leveling the pits into fields, causing the thorny wastes to blossom with flowers, and reducing the force of the currents to the scattering of arrows—
this illustrious Bhīmasena, traveling with such speed, brought Queen Lumadevī before her husband in six days, covering the distance that would otherwise have taken a month.

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the illustrious Svāmī departed from the city of Kāśī for his own city, joyful at the satisfaction of Viśveśvara. Having conquered the native disputants of Kāśī—whose bodies were formidable as they were—just as Madhuripu (Kṛṣṇa) conquered the Vādirājas and took away their fresh butter, he likewise seized the splendor of that region. Like one fleeing out of fear of the cowherd women, he proceeded toward Lumaḍī, with Bhīmasena following in approval.

(68) Together with the sons of the illustrious scholar Vajranātha, those named Śrīraṅganātha, who had been commissioned by Bāhādūra Yuvarāja Sāha; and having resided for a long time in Kāśī along with the astrologers Dāmodara, who were connoisseurs of the poetic play of the illustrious Lord of Ḍillī; and accompanied by the blessings of the city’s priests, Raṇabahādūra entered his own city.

(69) Hail! The illustrious Bhadrakālī, the divine Lumadibhagavatī, perceiving the King as her own protégé, rose up swiftly as if eager to welcome him with an advance greeting. She created a canopy with various banners and cloths raised on tall poles, while her face was made resonant by the auspicious whistling of the hollow bamboos, out of a desire for his welfare.

In the forest fragrant with *kadamba* trees at the seat of modesty (*lajjāpīṭha*) and the field of *vajratuṇḍī*, where the goddess Śrī Bhadrakālī—accompanied by the divine Lumahibhagavatī and Vajratuṇḍī—is present, she scatters leaves and flowers from *kadamba* blossoms shaken loose from branches by the wind. Amidst the war-cry blasts of the birds dwelling in the trees crying out, "By good fortune! May it be well for me!", [the goddess is worshipped]. (137)

(70) In the midst of the cavalry of horsemen, the heroic King Svāmirāja, followed by Bhīmasena, moves about secretly. Bearing the splendor of heroes, he carries two swords with fierce jeweled hilts held in his two arms;
with the luster of those unsheathed blades, his form appears manifold as if permeated by the Upaniṣads. May he offer that very prostration which was previously performed by Ajana to Bhadrakālī.
Having concentrated his mind and awakened Viṣṇu reclining upon the waters, the Creator praised Yoganidrā in order to slay the demon Madhu-mukha, as well as Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa;

and likewise, in order to destroy the freshly enraged Mahiṣa along with his army, the Lord Śrīsvāmī—the king of yogins and author of the hymn to the Goddess Lumuḍibhagavatī—praises her with the words "Hā Smā. (139)

(71) Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Homage to the illustrious Eight Mothers. May there be well-being! O Bhadrakālī, Lumuḍibhagavatī, Vajratuṇḍī, Viśālā, and the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī—you who remove the sins of living beings, may you remain here as those who are grateful.

May you, the assembly of the Blessed One, dwell in Nepal, the land of merit; I am your servant, and may you, being gracious, release me from this innate fear of worldly existence, which has become my very boundary. || 140 ||

O Blessed One, you are the destroyer of distress and calamities; you are Tāriṇī, known as Saṅkaṭā; you are inaccessible even within the sacred traditions (Āmnāyas), and among the primary elements (Prakṛtis) you are the discordant one, knowable only through the diversity of your names.

Seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus in your hand, the whip for the horse of Death, the one difficult to reach who destroys misfortune—you are the Mistress of Nepal; you are both male and female, yet you are joined with the ages of Kali, Dvāpara, and Tretā.
O Goddess Vajratuṇḍī, this land under your jurisdiction is now called Tuṇḍīkṣetra; it produces shame in the minds of the wise regarding their misdeeds.

For your sake, the Siddhas brought from the snowy peaks the summit of medicinal herbs; therefore, with my head bowed low, I bow to you, the Queen of Physicians, for the diseases born of one's own nature. (72) 142.
O Śrī Tuṇḍībhairava, you who hold a skull-cup in your hand, wear a crown, and carry a staff—by the grace of your lotus feet, Ralla and Malla experienced supreme bliss in the past.

Even today, O Mahākāla, you bring fulfillment to meditative contemplation; since you are the unshakable form within the kingdom of your sons, may you destroy our sins—you are our refuge, you are my mind. 143.

May Brahmāṇī protect us—she whose face is as radiant as gold, who sits upon the back of a swan marked with a wheel, holding in her hands a book, a rosary, a water-pot, and the gesture of fearlessness; adorned with shimmering earrings and blazing with ornaments on every limb; she whose object is attainable through the meditative absorption of the knowledge of Brahman. (144)

(73) He took refuge in the consort of Maheśa, who is as white as snow, jasmine, and a conch shell; whose luster is like the rising moon; who is mounted upon the bull; who possesses three eyes; and who is the progenitor of the three *guṇas*.

With her hands, she holds a sharp trident—the cause of the creation and maintenance of the universe—as well as a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) that resounds with a fierce roar throughout the three worlds, a battle-axe (*paraśu*), and a noose (*pāśa*).

O Śrīkaumārī, who possesses the luster of the hibiscus flower and blood, protect me, who am wretched and reeling from the many fierce poisons of the serpents of sense-objects—she who shone with a spear and noose in her hands, bearing a spear and a banner, uniquely skilled at tearing apart hosts of enemies, and seated upon a peacock vehicle. 146.

I meditate in my mind upon the consort of Śrī Viṣṇu, who rides upon Garuḍa, who possesses three eyes, and who holds an enemy’s mace, a conch, and a goblet; she who is dark like a blade of dūrvā grass, who is compassionate toward those devoted to her, who destroys the path of the unrighteous, and who brings joy to her devotees—O Bhavānī, lead me, who am wavering, to the further shore of saṃsāra.

O Śambhu, may this Ambikā—whose hand is marked with the thunderbolt and banner, who sits upon an elephant, who wears a sunshade and a beautiful crown, and whose complexion is like the hue of saffron—be the bestower of the fruits of abundant devotion and liberation. May she forgive my repeated offenses; grant me your own abode at your feet.

May Ambikā protect me—she who has a face as dark and terrible as a rain-cloud, who raised up the surface of the earth with her fangs, who rides upon a buffalo, and who utters sharp cries; she who holds a sword and a goad, and who, endowed with four arms, bears a fierce pestle and a mace; she whose hair is tawny like a peacock’s crest and stands upright, and who is radiant with a blooming red hue.

May the goddess Kālī—who is the very essence of Time, who has swallowed the night of destruction, whose body is as dark as a multitude of clouds, who is the Skeleton, whose ears are black, whose veins are prominent, and whose limbs are adorned with garlands of skulls;

who, standing upon a corpse in the cremation ground, wields a sword and a trident while shouting aloud—protect me, who am terrified and seeking refuge, she who holds a fruit in her hand and is the Death of the hosts of Time. 150.

O Mother of the World, O Mahālakṣmī! With a pair of lotus-feet adorned with tinkling anklets, with brilliant earrings shining at your ears, and adorned with most beautiful jewel-ornaments, you are the protectress of the three worlds. Bearing a sword, a lotus, a shield, and a skull-cup, and seated upon a lion—dispel the scorching heat of the fire of poverty! 151.

I worship Mahābhairava, who has three eyes and a crest of moonlight; whose topknot of matted hair stands erect; who brandishes a sword and shield upon his chest while roaring against a Vetāla; and who has surpassed the roar of the three-headed Kālī by being strengthened by the bellowing of a living bull and a black antelope skin, which are splashing with the overflowing streams of nectar from a vessel filled with ambrosia.
When you, the eight Mothers, are pleased, there are the eight great supernatural powers (*siddhis*); when you, the eight divine Mothers, are angry, there are the eight great terrors.
For those who hear, read, accept, or grasp this song, it shall for a very long time bestow glory, spiritual accomplishment, and wisdom. (153)

(76) Thus, O eight Mothers—O Śrīlumuḍi, O Blessed One, O Śrīmahākālavīra-devī, O Śrīvajratuṇḍi, O remover of natural fear, O you who destroy distress in times of peril; O Goddess Pratyaṅgirā, O Blessed One, O you uniquely skilled in destroying the magical spells of others—do not now render my petition like the accidental markings of a woodworm! Homage to you all! 154.
O Śrī Mahārājarāja, who bestows well-being and all perfections upon the battle with the gods and upon your circle of ministers and forces;
O Blessed Mother, when the mind is fully satisfied, who is wealthy and who is poor? I pray for nothing but single-minded devotion. 155.
Victory, O Lord, sole object of worship for the universe! Victory, O you who are adorned by the king of serpents!
Victory, O Śambhu, Lord of Gaurī! Victory, O you whose crest is the crescent moon! 156
Victory to you, who resemble ten million suns; victory to you, the abode of infinite qualities!
Victory to you, O Rudra, the three-eyed one; victory to you, the eternally stainless one! 157
Victory to you, O Lord, ocean of compassion! Victory to you, destroyer of the suffering of devotees! Victory to you, O Master, who carries us across the difficult-to-cross ocean of saṃsāra! 158
Be gracious to me, O Mahākāla; having brought about the destruction of all my sins, protect me, O Supreme Lord, who am weary of saṃsāra. 159.
Satisfied, Śrī Bhadrakālī, the Blessed Lumuḍibhagavatī, Vajratuṇḍī, Viśālā, Śāntā, Pratyaṅgirā, and the heroic Mahākāla— whose head was consecrated by the sage Akṣobhya—

each offered their own innate form to the Lord for the destruction of the race of Danujas, amidst the sounds of "Hā Hā" and "Hu Hu" arising from the thundering of dense clouds in the sky like a stormy day.

Having received from the goddesses, who had assembled together, a form and a weapon capable of bringing widowhood to the multitude of wives of his enemies' clans, the majestic King Raṇabhaṭṭūra Sāha— like Indra, the son of Kṛtavīrya, possessing a thousand arms and eyes— became the cutter and destroyer even of those enemies who had taken refuge in the abode of Bali.
As King Raṇabāhu approached the city gate, he entered the mansions where young women spoke with joy and where festivals of song had begun;

there he was met with auspicious blessings from the citizens, whose faces were drenched in the tears of joy produced by their eyes—which served as consecrated rice—and with fragrant scents mixed with the longing for his welfare. (162)

Having reached the palace, Raṇabhadra, though his fatigue was overcome, was filled with indignation; yet, smelling the exquisite lotus-face of that jewel among men and offering consolation, he quickly cast off the grief arising from Kanakāvatī’s departure upon seeing the Goddess Tripureśvarī, the Blessed One, massaging her lotus-feet.
"O Goddess, O beloved, O passionate one of beautiful character, may you prosper by good fortune upon this earth!
Thus, with eyes closed due to his endearments, he spoke of his own experience felt through love.

(79) Just as Kauśalyā was to Daśaratha, Arundhatī to the sage Vasiṣṭha, Jānakī to the Lord of the Raghus, Menā to the Lord of Mountains, Svāhā to the Fire-god, and Śrī Viṣṇubhakti to the Trident-bearer, so did that queen Tripureśvarī address Raṇabahādura, her beloved. 165.

O son of Sāhadeva, having conquered the western lands and their measured hosts of kings, as well as the eastern territories never before subdued, and having now spent time in Kāśī, our kṣatriya birth has been made fruitful today; salutations to the Blessed One of immeasurable valor!
Then, having embraced his son, the King shone like Lord Śiva with Gaṇapati after the battle of the gods; he was like a forest fire to his enemies.
(80) Indeed, while burning the root, protecting the trunk, and nourishing the flowers and fruit, is it not as if a tree near at hand has become a source of heat from afar? 167.

Having summoned those known as the *Arjyāl* path-finders, the six *Akāvas*, those called *Tathāpāh*, the *Pāṇḍes* who speak with names of unerring and manifest meaning, the *Rāṇās* who determine the principles of statecraft for the king, the lord of Gorakṣācala, and also the *Boharas*, he reached a decision. (168)

Those who were unfaithful toward their wives while their husbands were away on long journeys, those who obstructed the paths and moved treacherously in every direction—having ripened through sins born of many lifetimes, they now sink into this mire of excrement, urine, and pus, bound by the unrefined threads of their own karma within this endless calamity. (169)

(81) Then, having fashioned a powerful wooden wheel bound with a series of mechanical levers and fastened to the neck, he placed it upon his subjects—how truly heart-rending was that for one so distressed!
For even at the neck of a single horse, as if from an enemy, there was the constant falling of sword-blades, alas, due to the hostility of Raṇabaha, Dūrasāha, and Pratīpa. || 170 ||

A certain Pūtanā-like nature, known as Pānakaumārikā, who was hostile toward the *prakṛtis*, highly esteemed Lord Rāja—who was staying in Kāśī and wandering in solitude—and, having made her own retinue of donkeys into captives, drove them along with her son; she performed intense penance on the slopes of the Himālaya mountains, like the daughter of that mountain. || 171 ||

(82) Those female gatekeepers whom Śūrpaṇakhī had appointed as warriors in battle were suddenly deprived of their noses and hair by the illustrious Rāma, like a night-stalker woman. Then Śaṅkhadhara, a traitor who followed the ways of a servant and had strayed onto the path of unrighteousness, quickly offered his head as an offering of resinous incense, in accordance with his own nature. 172.

Thus, all those who were oppressed by Raṇabāhadūra became his enemies; they all swiftly became guests in the abode of Vaivasvata (Yama). Having thus crushed his foes, King Śrī Raṇabāhadūra commanded Bhīmā, sending the people of Kāśikā toward the eternal state.

"From this day forward, even half of my own portion has been granted to you as a noble station by me; for you, Bhīmasena, the crest-jewel of the assembly of ministers and well-wisher of the king, are now one whose body consists of half of my dharma and who is solely intent on meditation upon my feet.
Thus, O Bhīmasena, you are successful in the undivided kingdoms of my son, the illustrious lord of the gods."

(83) Having received abundant grace from the illustrious Śrīgīrvāṇamahīpatīndratilaka, the venerable Raṇabāhadūra Raghupa, like Rāma protecting Laṅkā, has now forcibly arrayed the host of the army named Kampū and presented it as an equivalent of an akṣauhiṇī to Bhīmasena. 175.
Through the repeated stamping of seals, the price of ink-stones rose manifold; likewise, for the writing of characters suited to those various documents, there was a great demand for paper and ink.
Yet, even when recording the *mārphat* script upon those respective leaves, no weariness arose in this illustrious Minister Bhīmasena, the jewel of the Thāpā clan, who remains ever-victorious. (176)

(84) "The laws of family and country must not be transgressed by a wise king who regards the teachings of the scriptures"—it was with this very understanding that Bhīmasena served as an informant; may he, who acted for the benefit of his master, be long victorious and renowned. 177.

Formerly, those great lords—Hārītī, Śītalā, and others, as well as the Liṅgas of the quarters, Tuḷajā, Bhairava, and the Kṣetrapālas—their splendor had been eclipsed and their worship abolished by the illustrious Svāmin.

Yet, through the application of logic and political strategy by Bhīmasena, that jewel among ministers, all of them regained their respective forms of worship, having had their rites restored at the word of King Raṇabahādura.

(85) It is no wonder that even those kings who were like Indra, who had crushed their adversaries and possessed great energy, and whose circle of ministers—even those of the highest wisdom—vied with one another for excellence; they too did not abandon here this succession of royal duties, serving as the ground for the written commands of King Hariścandra, the lord of men, who was like Brahmā himself. 179.

(86) They cross the oceans, they follow every direction, they climb mountain peaks, they enter wildernesses, they traverse the surface of the earth—surely these are the deeds of those whose path is never obstructed by anyone when following the worlds of their past actions until their enjoyment is exhausted, like waves entering the subterranean realm. 180.
That long vine of karma is ever-renewing, filled with ancient floods of fruit, possessing a wondrous form, constantly following embodied beings, and remaining steadfast;
it is drawn out, made to sit, then split, uprooted, or crushed by various merits, yet even when reduced to the most subtle particles, it never goes to destruction. (181)
That this moon bears upon its lovely body a dark and heavy disc of defects, that it possesses a cruel-formed serpent whose rays are matted like hair,
and that it displays to the kings a variegated life through various forms— this is surely the line of destiny’s creation, rich in the transformation of the sequence of wonders.
(87) King Dharma, whose essential nature had been made an object of scrutiny by Citragupta, was surrounded on all sides by the King of Love;
King Svāmī, whose burden had been taken up by Bhīmasena, was likewise surrounded on all sides by the other kings. 183.
Indeed, within the bellies of the worlds of the three realms, the ripening of the karmas of living beings bears fruit;
for where is the one who is far from the arms of the king’s warriors in battle, and where is the one who is far from the natural enemies, the *serabāhas*? (184)

Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā during the rainy season, and having entrusted his own body along with the illustrious Gīrvāṇayuddha to Bhīmasena—who is straightforward by nature and possesses the great valor of a king—King Kṣitiparaṇabahādura attained the stainless state that transcends duality, remaining above his own refuge; thus the glorious Bhīmasena, who protects the king’s command and is devoted to the monarch, reigns supreme. 185.
King Pālpyo, Vidursāhasera, Bāhādūrsāh, and the minister Nṛsiṃha—those who were brought by Niṣādas with a single rope and were indeed decapitated for their task—to them be salutation! (186)

Those who were traitors to their lord, hostile to the service of the king, and who, out of sight, plundered the wealth and attendants of others like owls; those whose sacred bathing places were frequented by outcasts (pulkaśas), and whose limbs were carried by water-fowls, cranes, wolves, dogs, and jackals—in the year of Śrī [1693], alas, only those virtuous and grateful ones remained! 187.
(89) Queen Śrīrājyalakṣmī, having previously departed from the Kaṭahara forest and by good fortune, through the power of her service to the Lāmā gurus, was reciting the *akṣamālā* mantra;

May he, who is skilled in battle, be victorious for a long time, being joyfully honored with blessings and showers of wealth by the delighted citizens.

(126) On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, under the Hasta constellation, on a Saturday, and during the sixth, eighth, or eighteenth year, the King of Kings bathes together with his mothers in the glorious and unfathomable Maṇisaras lake.
Worshipped there with royal splendor, Maṇiliṅgeśvara bestows upon that King of Kings, the sovereign of men, a wealth of children equal to himself, through hands in the form of flowing waves.
Fearing that his excessive majesty might dry up the ocean, the yellow-robed Lord [Viṣṇu], desiring a place of residence, entered King Rājendra;
for Lakṣmī took refuge in his treasury, Sarasvatī in his speech, the king of serpents in his sword, Fire in his majesty, the lord of horses in his horse, and the Moon in his crown.
When the auspicious conjunction occurred in the year six-eight-elephant-earth (1886) on the seventh day of the festival of Durga, which was a noble birth-day for King Surendra-vikrama,
Śrī Pṛthvinārāyaṇa— drier of the ocean of poverty for the three worlds— descended upon this circle of the earth with his six lineages as if they were his six limbs.

(127) Just as at that time there were abundant harvests of fine rice, barley, wheat, and other crops; great riches of *kaṅgu*, beans, *satīna*, mustard, sesame, and sugarcane; clouds raining at the proper season; trees laden with clusters of blossoms and fruits; and cattle yielding copious milk—at this festival of birth, all these things exist. 270.
While the illustrious King Pratāpasāha Siṃha ruled the circle of the earth, there was again and again the acquisition of cattle, land, gold, jewels, minerals, and silver;
this world, abounding in cotton, rejoiced within its bounds. Likewise, the auspicious day of the birth of the illustrious Yuvarāja bestows all prosperity and noble goals. (271)
When the earth has been made beautiful with various paintings by Hari and Hara, becomes a fit dwelling for the virtuous, and is served by the wise;
and when, with the neighing of horses that surpasses the skillful roar of clouds, it outshines the splendors of Mount Kailāsa with its own brilliance—then [it truly flourishes]. (272)
(128) Even the Lord of Wealth and the Master of Yakṣas, having recognized the true disposition of the King of Kings, abandoned their pride regarding their own splendors.
"Kailāsa has been surpassed by my white palaces with their crescent moons; my friend Caitraratha forest and the city of Alakā have been eclipsed by my groves. 273.
(129) By means of the four renowned human goals that had approached him, the illustrious Raṇabahādura became a sovereign among the lords of the earth, complete in every respect.
With a portion not less than that, he was the king of the gods in the three worlds; and by his prosperity, Rājendranṛpati here on earth possesses full splendor.

(130) Radiant with the power of his virtue, may this lord of men, the illustrious Mahārājarājendra, who is protected by the Fortune presiding over Lalitā Tripurasundarī, and who is exceedingly shielded by the Bhīma Thāpā family along with the Jaṭharakula, live for a hundred autumns here by good fortune together with the glorious Surendra. 275.

May the five great-grandsons of the illustrious and prosperous Śrī-Samṛddha—those who are the lords of the earth, the conquerors of all the kings of the world, the Mahārāja Sāha Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa, whose lineage extends from one shore of the ocean to the other—be victorious, their minds forever liberated from the dualities of the exhaustion of the labor of protecting the earth and filled with equanimous happiness. (276)

In beauty, he is Madana; with a gracious countenance, he delights the subjects through statesmanship; he is the subduer of enemies and the tamer of the host of the wicked; he gladdens the hearts of the gods.
He is the progenitor of the illustrious Lord of Dillī, Vīrasena; he is the destroyer of poverty; and he is the illustrious Rājarājārjuna, to whom wealth was offered by Thāpā Bhīmabahādur. (277)

(131) He who has surpassed the sun with his majesty, who creates the splendor of the moon with his face, who is a mine of virtues for the lord of the earth, who bestows honor upon the assembly of his own kin, who removes the addiction to poetry [in others], and who causes fever in the hearts of his rivals—oh, what a lord is this grandson of the sovereign King Raṇabhadra! 278.

May this illustrious Yuvarāja, who is like a boat for crossing the great ocean of poverty, remain for a hundred years; for he has been repeatedly sought out by me among the Jina and Jaina kings through the recitation of the names of the five "jewels" of men who support the world. May he bring me well-being! (279)

May the lords of Matsya protect you—those who are like diamonds among the rows of jewels in the treasury of the earth, who are as Bhīmasena (terrible in power) and possess heads as bright as the moonlight; who are priceless in the marketplace of the three worlds by the merchant-princes [of merit]; who are indestructible by the deceptive measures of those with arrogant and perverse steps; and who are the incarnations of the virtuous and the devoted ministers of the people.

(133) Once in the past, that Pracaṇḍaśivabhairava— who never before, since the beginning of the Kṛtayuga, had wandered elsewhere on pilgrimage while abandoning his own path, and who was the protector of the sanctuary named Śikharin— arrived at the city of Kāntipura, causing thousands of people to marvel.

(134) Having performed various rites of worship with the nectar-like words of the lord of the earth, he was escorted by the doorkeepers, chamberlains, and others from Dvārakā to the presence of the descendant of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and on the Saturday coinciding with the new moon day of the month of Nabhas, he was conducted there by the people.
"O King, receive a second crown prince," said Pracaṇḍaśivabhairava, and he withdrew like the king of birds.
Then, on a pure lunar day during the month of Pauṣa in the year of the Rākā bird, a second crown prince, endowed with auspicious marks, was indeed born.

By the command of the illustrious Lord Raṇabāhadūra, who attained the rise of his favor through the bearing of the burden of the constituent elements of sovereignty and who possesses the foremost martial prowess of the gods, the region where the minister of the King of Kings named Śrī Bhīmasena resides—namely the land of the Boṅkoṭa mountain—has now become known as Rājanvatī. (283)
In the three cities, at the crossroads where the quarters were ablaze, jackals howled at night with great piteousness, facing the direction of the fire;

this occurred on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, on a Wednesday, under the asterism of Āśleṣā, in the year measured by the three, eight, and moon (183). This was a constant omen indicating impending calamity.

(135) For in this Kali age, there shall be no lineage that has not been written off by the flood of falsehoods—never experienced before and yet destined to come to pass—given the scriptural accounts of its manifold calamities.
Only that family is truly a noble family which, having plunged into the ocean of King Pṛthvīnārāyaṇa’s forgiveness, remains ever pure and never touches the bottom.

In the year [1888], during the month of Māgha, on the dark lunar day of the Antaka-tithi (the fourteenth), under the asterism Śravaṇā, and on a Monday, Lalitā Tripurasundarī entered the penance grove— a refuge fashioned by the sons of Raṇavīrasiṃha, the lords of Urasā, for the destruction of the suffering of the three worlds.
Thus ends the Jewel of Nature in the *Śrītriratnasaundaryagāthā*. (136)
